title: Cryogenic Electron Tomography of Synthetic Layered Magnetic Organics
content: Electron dose limits fundamentally constrain the resolution of scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) tomography. 3D reconstruction resolution scales inversely with dose assuming a weak contrast approximation and requires both sufficient signal to-noise ratio (SNR) per projection image and high (>60 projections) angular sampling [1-2]. These conditions often exceed the electron dose tolerances of organic materials preventing features on the scale of a few nanometers from being resolved [3]. While most metals and ionic solids can withstand electron doses ranging from 103-108 e-/nm2, organic compounds degrade when exposed to a few e-/nm2 [4]. Several damage mechanisms contribute to structural degradation, such as knock-on displacement, mass loss, and beam heating; however, the dominant mechanism for organics, radiolysis, leads to irreversible chemical and structural changes by breaking molecular bonds, thereby inducing volatilization and amorphization [5]. Cooling organics to liquid nitrogen or helium temperatures improves dose resilience by 2-13, although the exact improvement is not well agreed upon. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is essential to nanometer 3D resolution in organometallic specimens [5-8].
